question_text: Under Republic Act No. 6713 (Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees), what is the statutory requirement regarding Divestment of Business Interests?

options.text: Mandated under 60 days from assumption of office

hint_ladder.title: Orient yourself
hint_ladder.text: This question is about a specific deadline in RA 6713. Think about what the law requires a public official to do with any private business interests they have when they start a government position.

hint_ladder.title: The simple rule
hint_ladder.text: RA 6713 says that within 60 days of officially starting a government role, you must get rid of any private business interests that could create a conflict of interest. It's a firm deadline, not a suggestion.

hint_ladder.title: Apply it here
hint_ladder.text: Now look at the options. The correct one will mention that 60-day window from when you assume office. The wrong ones will try to make the rule seem optional, delayed, or limited to only certain types of officials.

hint_ladder.title: Almost there
hint_ladder.text: The law doesn't make exceptions for appointive officials, and it doesn't let you wait until retirement. It applies to everyone—elective and appointive—right from the start. Which option captures that?

A.text: Correct. RA 6713 Section 8(b) clearly states that public officials must divest from private business interests within 60 days of assuming office. This is a mandatory, non-negotiable rule designed to prevent conflicts of interest from day one.

B.text: This one is tempting if you think appointive officials might have different rules, but the law makes no such distinction. Divestment is mandatory for everyone—appointive or elective. There's no opt-out clause.

C.text: It's easy to confuse this with retirement rules, but divestment isn't something you can put off. The law requires it within 60 days of starting, not at the end of your career. Waiting until retirement would defeat the purpose of avoiding conflicts while in office.

D.text: You might think this only applies to elected officials since they're more visible, but RA 6713 covers 'all public officials and employees.' That includes both elective and appointive positions. The scope is broad by design.

next_time_rule: Remember the '60-Day Divestment Rule': within 60 days of assuming any public office, you must divest from conflicting business interests. No exceptions, no delays, no distinctions between elective and appointive.
deconstruct_text:
Let's walk through this together. The key is RA 6713, Section 8(b), which is all about preventing conflicts of interest. The law says that when you become a public official, you have 60 days from the moment you assume office to sell off or otherwise get rid of any private business interests that could clash with your public duties. It's a clean break so you can serve without divided loyalties.

Now, let's test each option against that rule. Option A says 'Mandated under 60 days from assumption of office'—that's exactly what the law says. Option B says it's optional for appointive officials, but the law doesn't give anyone a pass. Option C says it's only required upon retirement, but that misses the point entirely—the deadline is at the start, not the end. Option D says it's only for elective officials, but the law clearly covers everyone.

Here's a mental trick to lock this in: think of the '60-Day Divestment Deadline' as a strict countdown clock that starts ticking the moment you take your oath. No snooze button, no exceptions for anyone.
